meaningMnemonic: When you're in prison, your only task is to count every angle in your cell. You count the angles of the walls and ceiling over and over again to pass the time. How many angles could there be in a room with four walls? Picture it and try to count those angles now.

This is the radical for axe , since it looks like one. The two horizontal strokes are the head, the long left line is the whole edge of its blade, and the vertical line in the middle is its short handle. Kind of a strange axe, I admit, but an axe is an axe.

If you find a rib cage on the moon, it'll probably be blue . Why? 'Cause it would have to come from one of the moon's inhabitants (the Moon People), and they're all blue — you know, due to the frigid temperatures and lack of oxygen and stuff.
See the slide going into the dirt? What appears to be a slide here is actually a coffin , sliding into the dirt to be buried.

In prison, dreaming in bed is the only way to see color . Picture a dark, dank cell with four gray walls. Now imagine the colorful dreamscapes your bed would take you to every night. What a contrast! That's why a prison bed = color.
This radical already looks like a pair of rectangular feathers , right? I guess those short lines in each feather are like the filaments of the feathers.

You have the radicals for loiter, two, and barb. Someone who uses two barbs on you while you're loitering really wants you to GO !! GO on, stop loitering outside of my convenience store, ya dang kids!

Underneath that hat are two bars of gold , but under those there are some spikes. This is some kind of trap for people who try to take your gold. And why else would you make a trap? Everyone wants to protect their gold.
This is a very oddly shaped key , but it's a key nonetheless.

This looks like a stick-figure foot on the left kicking at something, which makes it the radical for kick . See the shin and foot swinging up for the kick? You can think of that part on the right as the edge of a ball that's about to be kicked.

Think of an old-style lantern . It's in a box-shaped holder lined with rice paper and sits on four legs (you can only see two from this angle though). You can imagine people using these before electricity, right? That's why this radical is a lantern.

This looks like something hooked around the corner of a mouth — it's a lip ring ! Use your imagination, because it's either a giant lip ring or a very small mouth. It's angular because kanji prefer straight lines, but try to picture it as the kind of studded, angular lip ring your trendy friend wore in high school.
This is the radical for meat . What's meat-like about this? Think of a nice square slab of meat with some beautiful 人 -shaped marbling lines in it. Seeing it now? Mmm, meat.

Under the hat there are two people meet ing in private. Look at them huddled up in there. They must have a reason to want to meet in such a private place, but that's not for you to judge. Maybe next time you have to meet with someone you'll hide under a hat with them too.
See the mustache going around the mouth? Man, I wish I could grow a sweet mustache like this. (Sure, the mustache looks a lot like the head radical here, but just imagine it as a mustache this time!)

See that lid on top? It's actually a flying saucer. "Take me to your leader," say the aliens inside, arriving from a strange-looking moon. When do you think you'd see something like this? At night . When people see UFOs or the moon, it's usually night. That's why this is the night radical.

Here we have the ground radical, with something underneath it. What likes lying in the ground, covered in mud? A pig ! Use your imagination and see if you can find the head near the top, the piggy tail at the bottom right, and the little piglets on the left, nestling up to this mama pig.
The towel is getting soaked with drops of liquid. That's because it's rain ing. Get your towels and other clothes inside before they get soaked through from this rain!
This kinda looks like a spine with some rib bones, don't you think? That's why this is the radical for rib cage .

See the person running (to the right)? That's why this is the radical for run . Just don't confuse this with foot ( 足 ). The head in this one has streaks around it because the person is running so fast.
There are a bunch of lines coming out of a mouth. Think of them as speech lines in a little speech bubble. Those lines represent the things you say .
This radical is a scooter . See the handlebars and the little light? And there's a platform at the bottom you can stand or sit on (if it's one of those nice motorized scooters).
Remember the eye radical? Imagine that's your eye now, and there's a drop of paint falling into it, making your eye color unique. Now it's what makes you you. It's what makes you your self .

A single drop ( 丶 ) is just water. But as soon as there are three, rising higher and higher, you know what's coming. A tsunami ! Think of those drops as wave crests. Three whole tsunami waves, stacking up? That's a big tsunami.
You have 十 plus 十 (never mind that the left one is kinda curvy)... What do you get when you add these two kanji together? You get twenty .

On the top part of the head ( 冂 ) radical, there is a horn radical with one extra spike in the middle. This is a horned helmet with one extra spike. Who were famous for having horned helmets like that? The Vikings! That's why this radical is called Viking .

A rice paddy and some dirt — dirt roads, in fact, because this is a village . Small villages like this are mostly rice paddies and dirt (roads), you know? You could even think of this as a bird's-eye view of a village.

You have the legs of a bird with wings outspread, landing in the mouth of her nest to rest. And when does she go back to rest? When the sun sets in the west ! Imagine all the birds flying home as the sun sets. That's why this radical means west. You could also see this as pi coming out of a mouth. Why would a mouth be talking about pi? Probably to figure out the curvature of the sun's path as it moves across the sky — to the west, always to the west!
You know Wolverine from the X-Men? He has three claws that come out of his hand whenever he needs to fight, not at all unlike the radical you see here.

The angle radical and the angle kanji are the same! Hints You gotta know your radicals first! Only then can you start to study these kanji from other angles — meanings, readings, all that good stuff. One angle at a time, you know?
readingMnemonic: To see those kanji angles from every angle , you cock ( かく ) your head to the side. Hints Kinda like how a dog cocks its head at an angle when it's trying to understand what you say. That's what you look like when you're studying radicals! Aww, you're so cute.

meaningMnemonic: The axe radical and the axe kanji are exactly the same, with one minor difference. This kanji is also used as the bread loaf counter , probably because bread was so big and hard in the past that they had to use axes to slice them. Hints Imagine you've gone back in time a good hundred years, and you're trying to count loaves of bread after each swing of your axe. Axes and bread loaves will become intertwined in your brain.
readingMnemonic: You imagined being back in time too good and now you're stuck using an axe to be a bread loaf counter for the Kin g ( きん ) of England. You aren't sure which king he is or when in time you are, but he's mean and keeps eating all the bread you cut up with your axe. Hints Imagine being stuck using an axe on bread while the King of England glares down at you, munching and spilling crumbs everywhere.

meaningMnemonic: The blue radical and the blue kanji are exactly the same. Additionally, this can also mean young . You can remember this because young people have potential as limitless as the blue sky! Hints Don't feel blue, you should know this kanji automagically!
readingMnemonic: You've been feeling really blue . Mostly because your skin, hair, and eyes have all turned blue. It was an out-of-the-blue transformation! But now someone places his hand on your shoulder and points at your sa ber ( せい ). It's blue too! You aren't alone! Hints You aren't sure how you or the saber turned blue, but at least you and your saber are a good match now, I guess.

meaningMnemonic: The leader has a book all about the human body . Knowing about bodies is a privilege. One that only leaders get—it helps them control all their subjects, like you. Hints Imagine looking down at your body and thinking, huh, I wonder what all that junk is? Oh well, I'm sure the leader has it all figured out in that book of hers.
readingMnemonic: The leader's body book also taught her about something very body specific: how to tie a tie ( たい ). You can't have a tie on your body, no no. Those are for the leader and her smart body. Hints Picture the leader, reading a book, putting a tie on her body. Look around at you and your family and your neighbors. You don't know what your body meat-bags do and you don't know how to tie a tie. Womp womp.

meaningMnemonic: The color radical and color are the same in looks as well as in meaning. Hints Color me pink! This kanji's super easy if you know your radicals.
readingMnemonic: You already have color on the mind because you know the meaning of this kanji, so think of something colorful about yourself. Imagine your ear ( いろ ) being a weird color... green, purple, red, whatever. Just make it really bright and standing out. Hints You can even have someone ask you about your ear... "Is your ear okay? I think it's the color blue..."

meaningMnemonic: The ground is scattered with rice , which will cause the Predator to come because he loves rice. Then once he's gone, the next Predator will come to eat. Hints This kanji kind of looks like a Predator face, so just imagine Predators come whenever the ground is scattered with rice. They come from all around to grab handfuls of it. Who's next, then? Come forward!
readingMnemonic: When they come, though, they're all disappointed. It turns out it's rye ( らい ) grains, and rye grains taste terrible. Yuck. Hints If you love rye grains, on the other hand, imagine them being really happy that they came to get the rice. They're so lucky it's rye!

meaningMnemonic: Plant a spirit in the dirt before you start your company and it will be successful. That's what all the great, old Japanese companies did back in the olden days. That's why companies like Mitsubishi have been around for hundreds of years. They planted a spirit in the dirt to help their company grow, and grow it did! Hints Picture a young person way back in old-timey history times burying the spirit of one of their ancestors in the dirt. Now watch as an old-timey time lapse plays out in front of your eyes and a company is born!
readingMnemonic: Where did you learn about this method of company growing? From a sha man ( しゃ ), of course. Shamans aren't just spouting nonsense, they know what they're talking about. And spirits are right up their shaman alley. Hints Imagine going to a shaman and having them tell you that for your company to be successful you need to bury a spirit in the dirt so it can help the company grow. You should probably listen.

meaningMnemonic: What superhero is most like a triceratops ? …If you said Wolverine , you're correct ! Why is that the right answer? Because the triceratops has three horns, and Wolverine has three blades coming out of his hands. It's obvious, isn't it? But you knew that of course. Hints Picture a triceratops. Now picture Wolverine. An equals sign between them. A little arrow pointing at the horns, an arrow pointing at the blades. And a big flashing CORRECT sign above them. Need I say more?
readingMnemonic: Because you got the answer correct , you win a free trip to とう きょう . Congrats! Hints If you're lucky, you might see Wolverine fighting a triceratops in the middle of Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo. Heroes and monsters are always fighting in Tokyo, right? At least that's what my anime tells me.

meaningMnemonic: You have a mouth full of two massive drop s and… treasure ?! Upon closer inspection, they appear to form some sort of diagram ! Hints Scientists have spent decades trying to figure out what the diagram of two massive drops and treasure in your mouth could mean, but to no avail. Imagine the pain of having to spend your entire life with a mouth full of two massive drops and treasure… poor you.
readingMnemonic: After decades of analyzing the diagram , scientists found out it leads to… a zoo ( ず )?! Hints Now you’re stuck at this zoo with your diagram mouth full of two massive drops and treasure. Scientists think this can't be it, so further research will be required. Your diagram mouth of drops and treasure isn't off the hook quite yet. Just a few more years, spent at this zoo! I promise!

meaningMnemonic: You have a gun and you see some windows . What do you think you're going to do with this gun? Of course, you're going to shoot the windows... every single one of them. Each and every one. Hints Make sure you get every one, and don't miss any of them. Actually search around in your imagination for any more windows, because you want to stress it's important you hit each and every window with your gun.
readingMnemonic: Now that every window is broken, you feel pretty stupid because mi ce ( まい ) are pouring in through each one. You've made a way for mice to get into your house. That wasn't smart. Hints Now you need to shoot every one of the mice that came through those broken windows. You can't let any survive. You have to get every last one out of here!!

meaningMnemonic: The feathers radical and feather kanji are the same in looks as well as in meaning. Hints Have you been studying your radicals? If so, this'll be easy!
readingMnemonic: You've gathered feather after feather, like some kind of wannabe birdman or birdwoman, and now you're ready to fly. But as soon as you're about to take off, someone dumps honey ( はね ) on you, making your feathers all goopy. Hints Feel the honey in each feather, taste it trickling over your lips... And go ahead and plummet towards the ground (because you were jumping off a building to fly when someone doused you with honey). At least it's a tasty way to go, no?

meaningMnemonic: You have a tree and another tree . You basically have yourself a forest ! Hints Follow the logic of this one and you should be okay.
readingMnemonic: So, now you have this forest and you want to cut it down (so much money!). But, you don't have any tools, only your hands. You think... I've done karate for a while, so I can probably chop it down that way. You get in a chopping stance, then do your battle cry and hit: " HAYA... SHI****** ( はやし )!" Hints Obviously that didn't work well — you'll want to focus on your battle cry plus indecent swearing right afterwards to remember this reading.

meaningMnemonic: The go radical and the go kanji are exactly the same! Hints If you know your radicals well enough (and you do), you'll know this kanji.
readingMnemonic: "Oh, did he go again?" When こう いち is not around, that's what people often say because he goes to the gyo za ( ぎょう ) restaurant almost every day. こういち just loves gyoza so much, you always know where he is when he is not home. Hints Remember, whenever we see the reading こう , think of こういち , a founder of WaniKani (who loves gyoza). We'll keep it consistent, so over time you should develop a character around こういち that you learn to love or hate.

meaningMnemonic: The gold radical and the gold kanji are the same! Hints Just know your radicals and you'll be golden, so to speak.
readingMnemonic: The most gold in the land belongs to the Kin g ( きん ) of England. In fact, you've never actually met someone with gold, it all goes straight to the King whenever someone finds some. You just have a few pennies to work with. Hints Picture the King on a huge pile of gold. Gold coins, gold candelabras, gold ponies. He's laughing and pointing at all of it while making very strong eye contact with you.

meaningMnemonic: You plant your flowers in the light of the sun in the shape of a cross , but it's too hot — the sun is too strong — and you end up with grass . Flowers can't grow in these conditions. Hints Think of how disappointed you are. You wanted a beautiful cross of flowers, and now you just have a big overgrown patch of thick grass. It isn't even pretty green grass, it's a little brown and damaged from the sun.
readingMnemonic: The grass on top is brown and burned from the sun, so you need to take a cool saw ( くさ ) and hack the tops off. The saw is actually physically cool to the touch, to help heal the grass's sunburned bits. It just happens to look cool too. Hints Imagine using your cool saw to saw off the heads of all of this grass. You made the cross pretty big, so there is a ton of grass to get through. The sun is beating down on you and the grass too, which isn't making it any easier.

meaningMnemonic: The village you always think of first is your hometown . Hints Why would you ever talk about the village where someone else was born? Answer: you wouldn't. Everything is always about you.
readingMnemonic: Your hometown is where you sat ( さと ), nostalgia tugging at your heartstrings amid the endless rice fields and dirt. Hints Visualize yourself sitting in your hometown, the village's rustic charm evoking nostalgia.

meaningMnemonic: You see a triceratops in the distance. But, it's odd. It's perfectly pi shaped (that is, circular, like a pie). Some kind of piceratops, if you will. The reason they are this shape is because they want to absorb as much light as possible. They evolved to be round so they don't have any corners casting a shadow. Hints Absorbing light is natural for reptiles, and a round one can absorb even more. Imagine this strange, round piceratops basking in the warm rays of light shining down from the sky. What a rare sight you've come across.
readingMnemonic: As you watch this majestic beast absorbing light , suddenly several dozen feral こう いち s burst out from the wilderness, spears in hand. Oh no! Those こういち s are hunting this rare piceratops! Hints Imagine many different (but also kind of the same) こういち s attacking and throwing spears at the piceratops. Little do they know that it's fully charged up after absorbing all that light, and it unleashes a bright flash of energy, rendering all the こういち s momentarily blind and allowing it to escape.

meaningMnemonic: The leader 's key is the key that make s all the other keys. It's sort of like the one ring to rule them all, the one ring to bind them... except with keys. Hints Imagine the leader taking his key to open up a safe that has a button to make other keys for the underlings. No key is as great as this key, though.
readingMnemonic: The leader make s all the keys and puts them in a sack ( さく ) to distribute them to the underlings, who then cut them into shape with a saw ( さ ). Hints Imagine the leader making the keys and dropping them one by one into a big sack. He's always walking around carrying a big sack over his shoulder, distributing the keys to his underlings and watching them saw them into shape.

meaningMnemonic: How many evenings are there? There are many . Hints If you accidentally think "a lot" or something similar, that's okay too. It's the basic meaning that counts, and all these things are pretty close, though eventually you want to get to the point where you know that this kanji does in fact mean many .
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading た we use the word "taco." Let's start with the kanji meaning: many . You go outside in the evening (because that's what this kanji is made up of) and are surprised when you're hit by many ta cos ( た ) flying from the sky. For some reason it's raining tacos, and of course you have no idea why. Hints The tacos pelt you and knock you off your feet. Hard shell, soft shell, meat, lettuce, tomatoes, cheese... it's terrible. And there are so many of them, flying from the sky to drown you in tacos. This is absolutely absurd (and you should think that too, so you remember the reading).

meaningMnemonic: The meat radical and meat are the same in looks as well as in meaning. Hints Study those radicals, and perhaps we'll eat some meat tonight.
readingMnemonic: You know who loves meat ? Nick ( にく ). You probably know a Nick — imagine him eating some succulent meat right now. Hints If you don't know anyone named Nick, then just imagine it's Nic Cage. Picture him as he chews that succulent meat, maybe even closing his eyes in gastronomic ecstasy. Yeah. Go for it, Nic. Enjoy that meat.

meaningMnemonic: The meet radical and the meet kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: What better way to meet new people than to start kay aking ( かい )! Get into your kayak and just float out into the water. You'll eventually bump into someone else in a kayak and boom, you're meeting someone new! Hints "I met my soulmate in a kayak," said Koichi.

meaningMnemonic: You put a lid on your father . But, he won't taste good alone, so you mix in some other ingredients. They mingle inside the pot with him. Hints This may seem traumatic, but actually your father is surprisingly into it. Imagine him mixed in with all kinds of other things.
readingMnemonic: With a mix of your father and other ingredients mingl ing in your cooking pot, you lift up the lid... your father pops up. Your father is こう いち . He stares back at you with a big smile. Hints "I love mixing in with potatoes and tomatoes," your father こういち states. "Turn up that temperature. I like to mingle with a bit more tingle."

meaningMnemonic: Someone on a scooter has an axe , and they're getting near to you really fast! Oh no, they're so close now, you need to get out of here! Hints Picture a scooter coming toward you in the dark. You see the gleam of the axe as it looms nearer and nearer.
readingMnemonic: As they draw near , you recognize who is riding the scooter: the Kin g ( きん ) of England! Behind him, a bunch of his guards also on scooters and wielding axes appear and move close to you. Hints The King is now so near to you his nose and mustache are tickling your face. He's holding the axe high above his head and saying, "I can get as close to you as I want and you can't stop me because I'm the King. I can get sooooo close. Look, I'm not touching you though!"

meaningMnemonic: The night radical and the night kanji are exactly the same. Hints All those late nights studying radicals really pay off, you know.
readingMnemonic: You call your friend at night and say " Yo, Lou ( よる )!" Hints Lou is a total night owl, so you only hit him up at night.

meaningMnemonic: Who's someone who's just a mouth with legs ? That's your know-it-all older brother , who won't shut up about anything. Hints To help this mnemonic along, literally imagine your older brother as someone that's just a giant mouth with a pair of legs walking around. It talks and talks and talks, too, irritating you. Feel the irritation specifically at your older brother. He's older than you, so you can't beat him up... yet.
readingMnemonic: You wish you could box your loud-mouth older brother up and send him far away to きょう と . きょうと is super far away from where you currently live, so just ship your older bro off so he can never bother you again. Hints Hmm... don't you want to go to きょうと someday? Maybe you should have sent your brother somewhere less cool.

meaningMnemonic: When the moon is bright, it's easy to see that a pig is indeed a pig . Hints Imagine walking outside at night and seeing a strange oinking animal. You think it's a pig, but just to be sure you grab that thing and hold it up to the moonlight. Yes, definitely a pig! Now you know.
readingMnemonic: Legend has it that if you catch a pig in moonlight, it will tell you its secrets. Sure enough, this pig tells you it's from Bhuta n ( ぶた ). Hints A pig from Bhutan?! Yes, all pigs are actually from Bhutan, it whispers. Then this Bhutan pig escapes your grip and trots off into the moonlight.

meaningMnemonic: The radical for rain and the kanji for rain are the same thing. Hints Make sure you know your radicals!
readingMnemonic: What if the rain actually tried to aim ( あめ ) for you? As in, drops would move out of their normal flight path just to hit you on your head? You'd be a lot wetter, that's for sure. Hints Imagine a world where each rain drop had to choose a target to aim for. How strange would rainfall be? Also, あめ and "aim" don't really sound too much alike, but the goal is to use "aim" to get to あめ , so make sure to take note of that in your mind as you learn the reading.

meaningMnemonic: The rice radical and rice kanji are the same in looks and meaning. This kanji can also mean America , maybe because America is covered in rice or fields or something? Hints Aren't radicals nice? As nice and as fundamental as… rice. They make things so much easier, if you've been studying them.
readingMnemonic: A ton of rice is grown in America . And yet you never see rice in American cuisine. So where's all that unused rice going? Actually, it all gets dumped into a big bay ( べい ). They have too much rice and no place to store it, so they've started using bays to store it. Hints Imagine helping to bulldoze the rice into the bay, watching it fill it up, then pile high. A bay isn't the best space for rice storage, but it'll do. The important thing is that you think you have way too much of the stuff, so the only way to get rid of it is to dump it in a large body of water, and that large body of water is a bay.

meaningMnemonic: The radical run and the kanji run are exactly the same! Hints Make sure you know your radicals!
readingMnemonic: You run and run and run and suddenly you feel your sou l ( そう ) leave your body. Still running, you turn around and see your soul running a few steps behind you. Hints Running really takes it out of you. In this case, it takes your soul out of you. Don't worry, when you stop your soul will collide with you again and everything will be okay. (Probably.)

meaningMnemonic: There's a mustache on the ground . Upon closer inspection, you see that the mustache on the ground is exactly the same as yours! Hints Pick up the mustache, hold it up next to your face in front of a mirror. It's unbelievable, but it's the same in every way, down to the last hair.
readingMnemonic: When we need to remember the reading どう , we use the word "doughnut". While this is already strange enough, you notice something stranger. Over a couple feet away is a dou ghnut ( どう ) who also has the same mustache as you (and the one that fell on the ground). The doughnut looks at you for a moment, then scampers off. This doughnut must be a mutant because normally doughnuts don't move. Hints If it helps, imagine hundreds or thousands of doughnuts all around you with the same exact mustache. First of all, it's terrifying to be surrounded by thousands of mutant doughnuts. Secondly, it's really weird they all have the same mustache as you.

meaningMnemonic: The say radical and the say kanji are the same! Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: If you aren't sure what to say , just think about Gen ji ( げん ) and ask yourself, "What would Genji say?" Hints Genji is a real smooth talker. In fact, he can talk his way out of anything. If you can just stay calm and think "What would Genji say?" before saying anything, you'll probably end up saying something cool instead of something lame.

meaningMnemonic: The self radical and self are the same in looks as well as in meaning. Hints Radicals have self. Kanji have self. Kanji and radicals can sometimes be the same thing... so do they really have "self"? Only way to find out is to study both of them hard!
readingMnemonic: When we need to remember じ we use the word "Jesus." Who said you should always look at your self before tossing stones (or whatever) at others? Je sus ( じ ) did. So, make sure you look at your own self before being a jerk. Hints You can feel free to do some introspection here.

meaningMnemonic: You're walking at night when you discover a lantern covered entirely in hair , making it a very strange shape . In fact, this is a form you'd never expect a lantern to take. Hints Picture all the different shapes this hairy lantern could take in your mind.
readingMnemonic: You stare at the shape until you finally recognize it: ca ke ( けい )! Well, it's hairy, glowing cake, but it's still shaped like a big slice of cake. Hints Picture the shape of this hairy, glowing cake.

meaningMnemonic: You go down a slide made of branch es and your skin scrapes right off — ouch! Lucky for you, it was just your old outer layer of skin, and now you've got a fresh shiny layer. Yay for exfoliation! You're not sure what to do with this big, floppy layer of old skin, though… Hints Imagine sliding down a slide made of rough, gnarly tree branches. Their bark digs into your skin and pulls it right off of your body. Okay, it's painful, but it's a small price to pay for having such beautifully exfoliated skin.
readingMnemonic: Without your rough old skin to protect you, you feel the full he at ( ひ ) of the sun now. It burns… it burns! Yeah, you better protect that fresh new skin from the heat. Hints Your skin usually protects you from the heat, but imagine how raw it would be after you shed the old layer all at once. It's kinda vulnerable right now, so take care of it.

meaningMnemonic: What was the biggest hole in the construction of the world? The sky . If you think about it, the sky is like a big hole someone forgot to fill in. That's why this kanji also means empty ! Makes sense — nothing is more empty than the sky. Hints Next time you look up at the sky, try to imagine it's a big empty hole you're stuck at the bottom of.
readingMnemonic: The sky is usually empty until clouds stage a coup ( くう ). Basically you can think of the sky as the site for one coup after another as the weather changes. Hints First the sky's cloudy, then it's clear and empty, then overcast again... Just coup after coup!

meaningMnemonic: For some reason, you are stand ing on the sun . It's obviously very hot, but the thing you notice most is the sound of you burning up. Hints Imagine a super loud sizzling sound, drowning everything else out. It's ridiculously loud, and hurts your ears more than the sun's heat hurts your skin.
readingMnemonic: This sound isn't just loud, it's familiar. Finally you place it: on ions ( おん )! Hints Your burning body sounds just like sizzling, crispy onions being fried in a pan. Listen close. It's exactly the same! You can almost smell onions too!

meaningMnemonic: You have a wild viking child you have to take care of. He won't do anything but study , surprisingly. You can't get him to eat, use the bathroom, or anything else. He just wants to study. Hints Of course, this isn't what you'd expect of a little viking child. It's the opposite. That's why it's so surprising! He loves to study!
readingMnemonic: This crazy viking child who prefers study over pillaging (and other viking activities)... the other vikings just stop and gawk ( がく ) at him when they walk by. Hints You should tell the other vikings to stop gawking at this child. Just because he likes to study doesn't mean he's a bad viking...

meaningMnemonic: The leader for the ceremony can't come so you need to find a substitute ASAP! This kanji has another meaning too. The leader can't come to the ceremony because they fell through a time vortex into another era . They're trapped in a past era and don't know how to get back to the present, so a substitute will have to replace them in the ceremony. Hints Picture the substitute leader, looking all nervous as they get ready to lead the ceremony. Little do they know the real leader is fighting to survive in an ancient era.
readingMnemonic: The substitute leader is wearing the wrong color clothes, so you have to dye ( だい ) them — just like they did in past era s. Hints Imagine plunging your hands into a bucket full of dye and sloshing the substitute leader's clothing around in it, olden times-style. It's hard work, but it's not as bad as what the real leader's going through. Rather than dyeing, he's just dying… Dying to get back to the modern era!

meaningMnemonic: In a coffin there's a beggar , doing his begging. But it doesn't work, nobody helps him. So, he just begins to think : Why am I in this situation? How could I have avoided it? How will I get out? Think, dammit, think!! Hints Imagine him in his coffin, changing from a begging position to a stereotypical "thinking" position. His hand is on his chin, eyebrows furrowed. Focus on the beggar's thinking. This is a pretty abstract idea to imagine, so it will be important to create a vivid picture in your mind's eye.
readingMnemonic: What does the beggar think of? A thought bubble appears near his head. In it is a picture of こう いち ! He's thinking that if こういち were here, he'd save him. Oh, if only こういち could save us all! Hints Then, the beggar realizes that he is こういち . Here he is begging in a coffin, and still he only thinks of himself.

meaningMnemonic: There's a mouth inside a mouth . But if you look even closer (not actually, but we're pretending), you can see another mouth inside that mouth... and another one inside of that one! It keeps going and going. Can you count the number of times there's a mouth inside a mouth? This kanji also means revolve too. Think of each "time" a thing happens, it loops back around and comes back to the beginning, revolving around again another time. Hints Imagine yourself counting and counting smaller and smaller mouths inside of each other, recording the number of times you can find a mouth inside another mouth. Dig deeper and deeper until it feels ridiculous how small the mouths are getting. Be sure to focus on the counting and the number of times you find one. Now, how many mouths is this times two, because your mouth is like this too.
readingMnemonic: If you're having a hard time wrapping your head around the infinite number of times these mouths revolve , just picture yourself in a little kay ak ( かい ) going around and down through the mouths. Hints Your kayak is slashing and dipping through the revolving mouths, going down and down more times than you can count!

meaningMnemonic: Fins decorate a hat , with (presumably fish) mouths stitched to it. Who wears strange hats like this? Turns out, the valley people are the ones who wear these. I'm talking about the "Valley Girls" of Los Angeles, California. They're into the crazy fashion, and they'll wear anything if it's deemed "cool" or something like that. Hints Imagine a bunch of Valley Girls walking around with these strange hats. Fins and fish mouths... what a strange new fad.
readingMnemonic: Hanging around with all the Valley Girls in the sunny area of LA is also a robot. It's WALL-E's distant (and lazy, lounging) relative, TAN-E ( たに ). He sits around getting a tan in LA with the Valley Girls while his cousin picks up trash. Hints What a jerk he is. Imagine the deep tan lines on TAN-E as well. He's the epitome of robot laziness.

meaningMnemonic: You have a samurai with a flag on a stick . On his flag is the symbol 声 , the kanji for voice . Why does he have that there? He feels like his shogun isn't giving him and his fellow samurai a voice, so he's brought a flag with the word "voice" written on it to protest. Hints Imagine him and the other samurai with their flags on sticks, waving them around shouting things like "We want a voice!" and "Give us a voice!"
readingMnemonic: You decide to join the samurai's protest for more voice but immediately notice… they're all 子 , eh ( こえ )?! Hints Imagine your surprise at seeing this large protest of 子 samurai, shouting for their voices to be heard. Really make sure you can hear yourself going "You're a 子 , eh?!" in your head.

meaningMnemonic: The west radical and the west kanji are the same. Isn't that nice? Hints Make sure you know all those radicals, it will make your life more pleasant.
readingMnemonic: You go off to the west . It's the Wild West, even. There aren't many people out here, making it easy to find a niche ( にし ) for your snake oil business. Hints Imagine the dusty, ramshackle towns in the Wild West where you find your niche. You set up shops with big signs that say SNAKE OIL. Congrats, you've cornered the snake oil niche in the Wild West!

meaningMnemonic: Our leader has a lip ring . Wait, our leader has a lip ring? WHAT ?? Hints Think of our president (or your prime minister, or dictator, or whatever) and imagine this person appearing on television one morning with a big ol' lip ring. Feel surprised by it. Just say "What??" over and over again. You want to have the feeling of "what" in you when you imagine this — that'll help you to remember this kanji's meaning.
readingMnemonic: This leader with the lip ring wants one thing. What is it? A nanny ( なに ) who can make naan ( なん ). The leader loves naan because it's soft enough to eat with their lip ring on. And a nanny needs to make it because the leader can't do anything on their own. Hints Imagine this leader calling the nanny over. "What is it?" asks the nanny. "Naan!" shouts the leader. What would that leader do without their naan nanny? What indeed.

meaningMnemonic: You know what really sticks to your rib cage in the winter ? Wheat ! There's nothing like a hearty diet of wheat bread, Wheaties, and cream of wheat to get you through the tough winter months. Hints Smell the sweet, nutty aroma of wheat filling your home as you stockpile bags of the stuff to turn into bread and cereal. This winter might not be so bad, after all.
readingMnemonic: As you fill your home with wheat , it starts to get muggy ( むぎ ). You're in a small, enclosed area baking lots of bread and boiling a bunch of water for cream of wheat, so it's only natural that it would start to get pretty muggy in there. Hints You don't mind the mugginess, though — your muggy, wheat-filled house is actually pretty cozy during these cold, dry winter months.

meaningMnemonic: There is someone wearing horns , holding a bow , and going down a slide held up by a stick . What type of person do you imagine? I'd say someone who's an immature boy. That would be your younger brother . Hints If you don't have a younger brother, just pretend you do for now. Imagine him really vividly. He is a stereotypical little boy, playing dress-up with horns and a bow and arrow, and he's going down a makeshift slide held up by a stick.
readingMnemonic: Your younger brother loves playing dress-up so much that he's now started dye ing ( だい ) his hair all kinds of colors. Hints Imagine the bright red, blue, green and purple dye in your younger brother's hair. He's put so much on that he's dyed half his face too. He's going to be in trouble when he gets home!

meaningMnemonic: When you rest from school you are taking an absence from school . This is only for very long absences though, not a day or a week, but months or years. Think about it like taking an extended leave of absence from school.

It is the first answer, A ( あ ).

The すぐ part, however, is a new word, meaning "soon." すぐ and "soon" even start with a similar sound, so maybe that can help you remember this! If you put 今 and すぐ together, you get "now soon." Put in better English, that's at once or right now .

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of blue ? It's still blue ! It can also mean unripe , which might sound confusing, but it comes down to the fact that in Japanese there's some overlap between blue and green. So while in English we think of the "go" traffic light and unripe bananas as "green," in Japanese they're actually called "blue."
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to remember the あお portion to read this word. Think of blue things on your body. Those are bruises. readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. It would be a car raider ( からだ ). I'm talking about a dude who is a raider of some kind driving a car. If he runs into your body, you're done for, so watch out for the car raider. Of course, this mnemonic is only meant to get you close to the reading. Hopefully it is close enough to get you to the actual reading, からだ .

meaningMnemonic: What's a "third day moon"? It's a crescent moon . A crescent moon is the newly visible moon that appears on the third day of the month in the lunar calendar that Japanese people used back in the day.

Sounds complicated, but the changes actually make the word easier to pronounce. (Try it yourself — みかづき is easier to say than みっかつき , right?) Here's a mnemonic to remember the みか and づ parts, just in case: You're out with your friend Mika one night when a crescent moon appears. What do you say to her? " Mika , du de ( みかづ )! It's a crescent moon!" Hint: To get the character づ , type "du" on your keyboard.

meaningMnemonic: A big voice is a loud voice ! 大声 usually just describes talking in a big voice , but it can also refer to shouting depending on the situation.
readingMnemonic: The reading for 声 is ごえ (rendaku'd version of the reading you know: こえ ). The reading for 大 is the kun'yomi reading, like with the word 大きい ( おおきい ). Just imagine a loud voice saying " おお！ ."

sentences.english: I can't say too loudly that I joined the company through a connection.

sentences.japanese: 山の方に大声で「やっほー」と言うと「やっほー」と山びこがかえってきた。
sentences.english: When I said "Yahoo" to the mountains, a "Yahoo" echoed back.

meaningMnemonic: The big make ! What is your big make? Bigger than anything else. It is your major work ! 大作 means a large-scale, ambitious, or significant work. Depending on the context, it can refer to anything from an artistically accomplished masterpiece to a big-budget blockbuster movie.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Did you know that there's a monumental work about a tie sack ( たいさく )? It's a masterpiece about a magic sack that produces tie after tie after tie after tie... A bit like The Magic Porridge Pot, but with a sack and ties instead.

sentences.english: to write a masterpiece, to draw a masterpiece
to watch a masterpiece, to see a masterpiece

sentences.japanese: 「サイコ」はヒッチコックの大作だ。
「スターウォーズ エピソードI」は１９９９年のアメリカ一の大作でした。
sentences.english: "Star Wars: Episode I" was the most epic American film of 1999.

sentences.japanese: もう自分では大作のアイディアは考えられない。
sentences.english: I can't come up with any ideas for a masterpiece anymore.

meaningMnemonic: A man person is a man . There's a の particle stuck in the middle of this word. Here it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after. Don't worry if that's hard to remember though. Just remember 男の人 means "man" (and that it's more polite than plain 男 ).
readingMnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 4 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.

sentences.japanese: 田中先生は男の人です。

meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い on the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. What's the adjective form of many ? It is also many (or you could say much ). Speaking of which, there are so many kanji to learn, ammiright?
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Think of something that is many . Doesn't matter what it is as long as you imagine a ridiculous number of them. Many of them. So many that they start avalanching into you and crushing you. The last thing you yell is " おお !!!" as you get smushed.

sentences.japanese: ニューヨークは人が多い。
sentences.english: There are many people in New York.

sentences.english: This village is the most populated village in Japan.

meaningMnemonic: You have many part s. Look at them all. You have to choose one of the parts. You can't decide which one you want. This one? Maybe . How about this one? Hmm, maybe that one too.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 八月五日は多分休みですよ。

sentences.english: Meat is very important in my life.

meaningMnemonic: The お is an honorific that makes this word a bit more fancy. When you're talking about money you gotta be fancy, after all. So, you're basically saying "gold" in a nicer way. What was gold back in the day? It was money .
readingMnemonic: The reading for 金 is different from the one you learned with the kanji. Makes sense since this is a single kanji with hiragana attached. Here's a mnemonic to help you: You've saved up a ton of money. With it you're going to buy something awesome. Then, suddenly someone hits you in the knees with a bat. Now you have to spend all your money buying a cane ( かね ). Sucks for you :(

sentences.english: to have money, to be rich

sentences.japanese: ウェディングリングは、お金よりも大切です。
sentences.english: Wedding rings are more important than money.

sentences.japanese: 先月はギャンブルで多くのお金が入った。
sentences.english: Last month, I got a lot of money from gambling.

sentences.japanese: 本社のお金のマネジメントの仕方に不正があった。
sentences.english: There were some problems with the way of managing financials at the head office.

meaningMnemonic: The moon light is exactly what it sounds like: it's moonlight ! This word can also refer to a moonbeam .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 月 has two on'yomi readings, and the reading here changes from げつ to げっ , here's a mnemonic to help you remember how to read this one: Legend has it that the moonlight brings out a creature known as the Geck 光 ( げっこう ), an elusive species of gecko that shines in the moonlight. You've spent your whole life searching for this gecko. Now imagine spending yet another lonely night crawling around in the moonlit wilderness. Everyone thinks you're crazy, but you know you'll find that Geck 光 someday!

sentences.japanese: 夕べは、月光がとてもきれいでした。
sentences.english: The moonlight was very beautiful last night.

sentences.japanese: 白い月光がカーテンから入ってくる。
sentences.english: White moonlight enters through the curtains.

sentences.japanese: 月光の中に、月の王女がいた。
sentences.english: In the moonlight, there was a princess of the moon.

meaningMnemonic: The next month is the next month ! It isn't this month or the month before, it's the next one!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. 月 has two on'yomi readings, but since this is NOT a specific month name, it's going to use the げつ reading. Here's a mnemonic to help you remember that: Next month is when rye gets ( らいげつ ) into your diet. You're going to eat only rye bread and drink only rye beer for all of next month. Bet you can't wait!

sentences.japanese: ピアノのコンクールは来月ですか？
sentences.english: Is the piano competition next month?

sentences.japanese: 来月入社するスタッフは大体九十人です。
sentences.english: The number of new staff members who will join the company next month is about ninety.

meaningMnemonic: The next year is next year ! It isn't last year or this year, it's the next one!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to work hard next year too

sentences.japanese: 来年のプロジェクトまでは日本にいるつもりだよ。
sentences.english: I'm going to stay in Japan until next year's project.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

私は夜に出かけることが多いです。
sentences.english: I often go out at night.

meaningMnemonic: Eeh! Eh? ( いいえ ) No ! You’re so surprised by whatever the question was, you can only manage "Eeh! Eh? No!" in response. いいえ is a formal word for "no", so you can use it to answer politely in the negative.

sentences.japanese: いいえ、そうじゃないです

sentences.english: No, you have the wrong person.

sentences.japanese: いいえ、イギリスじゃないです。カナダです。
sentences.english: No, it's not England. It's Canada.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This implies that it is your older brother, by the way. Not somebody else's.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Your older brother is different from everyone else's. He has odd powers... some would say powers of the force. Do you know what his name is? It's Ani ( あに ), short for Anikin... wait a sec, does that sound familiar?

sentences.english: to be hard on one's big brother

meaningMnemonic: One’s self part is, after everything, still oneself . And the part that’s from my self is, well, myself . Everyone has their own part of their self. Pretty straightforward.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: You have the number "thirty" and the kanji 代 . You learned 代 means "substitute," but it can also mean era . What's the "thirty era"? It's one's thirties .

sentences.japanese: 三人の子どもが生まれたとき、父と母は三十代でした。
sentences.english: My parents were in their thirties when they had their three children.

meaningMnemonic: One times is one time . How many times? Just one.

sentences.english: Every month, I go to town for ramen at least once.

meaningMnemonic: You learned 空 means "sky," but it can also mean "empty." An empty car literally means "empty car," but in practice, you'll usually see this lit up on a taxi to mean open taxi . If you spot it, feel free to hail it down! You might also see 空車 at a parking lot. In that case, it means there's an empty parking space available.

sentences.english: In New York, if you see an available taxi raise your hand and shout, "Taxi!"

meaningMnemonic: You want to talk about the origin where something come s from. That's where it is from originally .

meaningMnemonic: Find a flat surface and go along it. Now you are running parallel to it.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: You have your body power . This is just another way to say physical strength . Watch out, if you use too much of your physical strength you may run out of physical stamina and endurance completely! They're tied together, so make sure to pace yourself.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Your physical strength and stamina are tied together with a tie lock ( たいりょく ). That's a lock made of ties that ties your strength and stamina up together, making it much easier to pace yourself.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

a man who brings the rain with him
the symbol for rain (on a weather forecast)
a woman who brings the rain with her

meaningMnemonic: What is real is right . It is the reality . It is also the truth . Don't believe anything that isn't real and true .

meaningMnemonic: The near year s are years that weren't too long ago. They're the recent years . Try to remember that 近年 is for the recent past (unlike 近日 , which is for the near future). sentences.english: These days, having a smartphone has become the norm.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. Note that this word refers to the grains of rice more than something that's a meal. If you're eating rice at a meal you'd call it ごはん . This is like when you're talking about the rice in the fields or rice grains or something like that.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: "Everyone, we have rice! Come ( こめ ) and get it!"

米は一キロ当たり五百円です。
日本で米が不足することは、あまりない。

meaningMnemonic: This word is the kanji same with hiragana attached, and it also means same . It's a bit of an oddball among Japanese adjectives, because you don't need な or い to attach it to a noun. So it's usually considered to be a "special" な -adjective. Have a look at the context sentences to see it in action!
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: When you think of the word "same" think same owner ( おな ). You're looking at a restaurant that has a sign that says, "New owners!" However, when you walk in you see it's the same terrible owner you remember from before. What a liar.

sentences.japanese: 毎日、車内で同じ人に会います。

sentences.japanese: マミちゃんと同じクラスになれますように。

sentences.english: to be born on the same day

sentences.japanese: どうして今日の空は水色なんだろう？
sentences.english: Why is the sky light blue today?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: Did you hear that sound ? It's barely audi ble ( おと ). Go ahead and say the word "audible" with the pronunciation of おと to help you to remember this.

sentences.japanese: これはフェラーリのエンジンの音だ。
sentences.english: This is the sound of a Ferrari engine.

sentences.japanese: 上のフロアから、大きな音がしました。
sentences.english: There was a loud noise from the floor above.

sentences.japanese: 雨の音がうるさくて、よく休めませんでした。
sentences.english: The sound of the rain was so loud I couldn't rest well.

meaningMnemonic: What shape has four angle s? The most common one is a square , but it could also be a rectangle or even a cube .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings for the kanji. You've learned them both already, so you should be able to read this word!

sentences.english: to fold something into a square

sentences.japanese: わたしのキーボードのキーは四角です。
sentences.english: The keys on my keyboard are square.

sentences.japanese: 日本の切手は主に四角ですよ。
「口」と言う字は、ただの四角に見えませんか？
sentences.english: Doesn't the character for "kuchi" look like a square?

meaningMnemonic: Who has a study life ? Only one person that I know of, and that's a student .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 母はメディカルスクールの学生です。
sentences.english: My mother is a medical school student.

sentences.japanese: 不正な学生ビザを用いて日本に来る人々もいます。
sentences.english: Some people come to Japan on fraudulent student visas.

sentences.japanese: 「人生の学生です」と言えば、学生のディスカウントがうけられるっていうのは本当なんですか？
sentences.english: Is it true that if you say you're a "student of life" you'll get a student discount?

meaningMnemonic: You have sun light . What kind of light would this be? Obviously sunlight .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since the にち reading of 日 becomes にっ here, we've made a mnemonic for you to remember this reading: The best place for sunlight in Japan is Nikkō ( にっこう ). It's one of Japan's most beautiful national parks, and the perfect spot to catch some rays!

sentences.japanese: このアパートは日光がよく入る。
日光に体が当たりすぎるのも、よくないよ。
sentences.english: It's not good to expose your body to the sunlight too much.

sentences.japanese: 北からは日光があまり入らないです。
sentences.english: There is little sunlight coming from the north.

meaningMnemonic: You have some gold ball s. What balls are more important than any other balls, at least for a dude? That would be his testicles . This word came about because tanuki scrotum skin would be used to pound down gold into sheets. Tanuki scrotums are apparently very good at this because they are very strong and very flexible. Strange, yeah? That's why Gold balls = testicles. As you might have guessed, this word is slang and you'll probably want to avoid using it at the doctor's! It's a comical word that is used in casual situations.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi for 金 and the kun'yomi for 玉 . If you know the readings of your kanji, you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: それは金玉ではありません。
自分の金玉が気に入ってます。
金玉は男の人の体の中でも大切なパーツの一つです。
sentences.english: Testicles are one of the most important parts of a man's body.

meaningMnemonic: Sorry ( それ ), can you grab that one for me? Yeah, that , thanks! You can use それ for things that are close to the person you're talking to, or fairly close to both of you.

sentences.english: I like that one, that sounds like a good idea

sentences.japanese: それ、おもしろそうだね！

sentences.english: Oh, you're going to go for that?

sentences.japanese: それはキャンディじゃなくて目玉です。
sentences.english: That's not candy, that's an eyeball.

meaningMnemonic: その means "that" or "the", and その plus other means things like the others , other , and other than that , depending on the context.
readingMnemonic: This has two readings, but luckily you learned one of them when you learned the kanji, and the other one when you learned the word 他 . The two readings are usually interchangeable, too.

sentences.japanese: その他のゴミはリサイクルして下さい。
sentences.english: Recycle the other kinds of trash.

sentences.japanese: その他色々なタイプありますよ。
sentences.english: There are many other types than this.

sentences.japanese: その他に元パートナーへ言いたいことはありますか？
sentences.english: Is there anything else you would like to say to your ex?

meaningMnemonic: The now times is this time .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 今回は、やめておきます。
sentences.english: I decided to pass this time.

sentences.japanese: 今回のオリンピックでは金メダルだった。
sentences.english: I got a gold medal in the Olympics this time.

sentences.japanese: 今回のトピックは「ロボット工学」です。
sentences.english: The topic this time is "robot engineering."

meaningMnemonic: What thousand ? Could be five thousand, two thousand, or ten thousand, since you're asking. Let's generalize. How do you say all of those amounts at the same time? You say " thousands ." If this is used in a question, it can also mean how many thousands ?
readingMnemonic: The reading is the kun'yomi なん for 何 and the rendaku'd on'yomi reading for 千 ( ぜん ) combined together. It's one of those weird words that mixes the on'yomi and kun'yomi readings.

sentences.english: several thousand vehicles, several thousand machines

sentences.japanese: 何千回もエラーが出た。
マミは人生で何千ものベーコンをたべてきた。
sentences.english: Mami has eaten thousands of bacon strips in her life.

sentences.japanese: この先、何千メートル行けばいいんだろう。
sentences.english: I wonder how many thousand meters more I should go.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading which you learned with the kanji. This is probably because this word gets attached to numbers usually, which makes it behave more like jukugo. So, you can have １回 , ２回 , ３回 , or even １００回 if you're into that sort of thing.

sentences.japanese: 今日はテレビを一回だけ見た。
sentences.english: I only watched TV once today.

sentences.japanese: これは犬用のボール。赤ちゃんのボールじゃないって、何回言ったら分かるの？
sentences.english: This ball is for dogs. How many times do I have to tell you that it's not a ball for a baby?

sentences.japanese: ファーストキスは人生で一回しかない大切なものなんだよ。
sentences.english: Your first kiss is an important event you only get to experience once in your life.

meaningMnemonic: You know this is a verb because it ends with an う sound. The kanji for this word is right or success , so what's the verb form of that? Turns out it's a ton of things. But it's mostly for when things go right. As in to be right or to be on target . 当たる is intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Your answer is right, or your shot is on target. See? No direct object.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you to remember the あ portion. When your guess turns out to be right , you can't help but shout, " Ah ( あ )!" That "Ah" is your victory cry.

sentences.english: the light hits, the light shines
the sun hits, the sun shines

sentences.japanese: テレビが当たるらしいよ。
sentences.english: Apparently you can win a TV.

sentences.japanese: やっぱりそうでしょ？当たってた！
やめろよ！人に石が当たったらどうするんだ。
sentences.english: Stop it! What if a stone hits someone?

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means see , and 見える is to be visible , or to be in sight , though it's often more naturally translated into English as can see . It's used when you don't actively intend to see something, it just happens. This verb can also mean to seem , when talking about how you perceive something you can see.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji (the kun'yomi reading). So as long as you know that you should be able to read this word as well.

sentences.english: to be clearly visible, to look clean

sentences.japanese: ここから火山が見える。
sentences.english: The volcano is visible from here.

sentences.japanese: あそこの村人が見えますか？
sentences.english: Can you see the villager over there?

sentences.japanese: 自分が他人からどう見えるのかがすごく気になる。
sentences.english: I'm really curious about how I seem to others.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means come so you know this word means to come .
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is pretty strange. It changes depending on the type of verb form you use (it's a pesky exception verb). To remember the reading of this word, here's a mnemonic: "I want you to come to the coo l ( く ) side, Luke," says Darth Vader. "What?" replies Luke. Just replace this line into the famous line from Star Wars. Say it out loud. Do the Vader voice. It'll help you to remember.

sentences.english: to come for the first time

sentences.japanese: オーストラリアに来る
アメリカから来ました。
お母さん、おねがいだから会社には来ないで。
sentences.english: Mom, please don't come to my office, I beg you.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means below , and 下がる means to get lower or to go down . It's an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. For example: Prices fall. Temperatures come down. See? No direct object. You can remember this because your fever always goes down when a certain girl ( がる ) takes care of you. Imagine a kind, caring girl making you chicken soup and giving you medicine and stuff — your fever would have no choice but to come down . (Also, this girl is probably your mom.)
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to use the kun'yomi reading. Let's use a mnemonic to remember the reading of the kanji: You were running a fever, but now your temperature has started to get lower . Why? Because you used a saw ( さ ). With your trusty saw, you did some good old-fashioned bloodletting, medieval doctor-style, and now your fever is really starting to come down. Actually, your blood pressure and oxygen levels have come down too… um, WAY down. Maybe using this saw wasn't such a good idea after all…

sentences.english: to go backwards, to step back

sentences.japanese: モチベーションが下がる
雨の日は気分が下がる。
sentences.english: My mood is lower on rainy days.

sentences.japanese: ベルトをしてなかったので、ジーンズが下がってきた。
sentences.english: I wasn't wearing a belt, so my jeans started to slip down.

sentences.japanese: 去年からスコアが下がった。
sentences.english: Scores have dropped since last year.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "life" so what is the verb form of that? Would it be "to do life"? No, probably not. In this case it is to give birth , or to produce . You'll have to differentiate this one from the word 生まれる as well. Just remember that when you give birth, you're the one who has to actually mo ve ( む ) your body by finding the right position and pushing with every ounce of strength you can muster. In contrast, when you're being born, you can just kind of lie there and enjoy the ride.
readingMnemonic: You have to remember the う part of this word to be able to read it. You already learned this reading with 生まれる , but here's a mnemonic for you just in case you forgot: Imagine yourself giving birth, but not to a baby. Instead, it's an u ni ( う ) you're delivering. Luckily, uni aren't fully formed with their spikes at birth so it shouldn't be a problem. Ooof! What a relief!

sentences.english: to give birth to a child
to give birth to a baby
to give birth to a puppy
to give birth in the mountains

sentences.japanese: ナツミは元気な男の子を生んだ。
sentences.english: Natsumi gave birth to a healthy baby boy.

sentences.japanese: このレストランのオーナーが、日本のイタリアンの人気を生んだシェフです。
sentences.english: The owner of this restaurant is the chef who made Italian cuisine popular in Japan.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means go so the verb form of this is to go .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to remember the い portion. To remember い we use the word "eagle." You want to go somewhere (anywhere!) but you can't. An ea gle ( い ) blocks your path. You try to go forward and it opens its wings and bites at you. You try to go back and it jumps at you. There's nowhere for you to go with this eagle standing there.

sentences.english: I'm going to Japan in November.

sentences.japanese: 他の用があるので、来月のパーティには多分行けません。
sentences.english: I've got other plans so I probably can't make it to the party next month.

sentences.japanese: タコベルがないなら月には行きたくない。
sentences.english: I wouldn’t want to go to the moon if they don’t have Taco Bell there.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means above , and this verb means to go up or to rise . It's an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. For example: Prices go up. Temperatures rise. See? No direct object. You can remember this because stock prices always seems to go up when you see this one girl ( がる ). You don't know how this girl makes stock prices go up, she just does. Think of her as your lucky girl.
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you can guess that it uses the kun'yomi reading. You've learned that reading, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher: You know this word means to go up or to rise . Imagine just rising into the air, sort of floating up all of a sudden. What would you say? You'd probably scream " Ah ( あ )!" the moment you started to go up. You know, out of surprise. Going up? Ah!

sentences.english: to go up all at once

sentences.japanese: エレベーターで上がる
sentences.english: to go up by the elevator
to go up by the stairs

sentences.japanese: エスカレーターで上がる
sentences.english: to go up by the escalator
Fireworks get set off in August.

sentences.japanese: 三フロア上までエレベーターで上がりましょう。
sentences.english: Let's take the elevator up three floors.

sentences.japanese: 去年よりコレステロールが上がってしまった。
sentences.english: My cholesterol has gone up from last year.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 入 means "enter," but this word does not mean "to enter" (which you already learned as 入る ). Still, the meaning of 入れる is still related to the kanji's meaning: it means to insert or to put in . It's something you do to another object, like inserting a key into a lock, or your hand into a glove.
readingMnemonic: When a vocab is a single kanji plus some okurigana (hiragana stuck on the end of kanji) it's almost always going to be the kun'yomi reading. This is one of two kun'yomi readings you'll be learning for the kanji 入 . As long as you know that this vocab means to insert , you can use that to remember the reading as well. Imagine inserting your hand into a hole and an ea gle ( い ) flies out, screaming: " い !" This is something that happens every time you insert your hand into something: an eagle comes out. You don't know why.

sentences.japanese: 毎日ボトルに水を入れる。
sentences.english: I put water in a bottle every day.

sentences.japanese: サンドイッチにアボカド入れた？
sentences.english: Did you put avocado in the sandwich?

sentences.japanese: ボランティアの会に入れて下さい。
sentences.english: Please let me join the volunteer meeting.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means study or learning . When you do these things, what ends up happening? You learn. That's why this word means to learn . There is another word that means "to learn" that is going to be more common, which is 習う . You'll learn this one later on. 学ぶ sounds a little more serious compared to 習う , so keep that in mind when you use it.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to remember the まな part to learn this word's reading. Think about a class you're taking. It's a manners class, and you're there to learn manner s ( まな ). Imagine this study of manners and imagine yourself practicing it.

sentences.japanese: 人生は学ぶことが多いです。
sentences.english: There are so many things to learn in life.

sentences.japanese: 兄はロボット工学を学ぶ学生です。
sentences.english: My brother is a student studying robotic engineering.

sentences.japanese: 学ぶことは大切だけど、多分もっと大切なのは、どのように学ぶかということ。
sentences.english: Learning is important, but perhaps what’s more important is how you learn.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means make . The verb form of that is to make .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Every time you try to make something, it ends up being too cool ( つく ). That's not an exaggeration. The stuff you make is literally too cool for the general public to see. They'd probably go crazy and start rioting, and before you know it society itself would collapse. No one's saying you need to stop making things, but please — hide your too-cool creations away somewhere. The world just isn't ready for them yet.

sentences.japanese: 母は、いつもサンドイッチを作る。
学生ポータルのアカウントもう作った？
sentences.english: Have you already created a student portal account?

sentences.japanese: ロボットを作りたくて工学のクラスをとってます。
sentences.english: I am taking an engineering class because I want to build a robot.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means meet so the verb form of that is to meet or to encounter .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to remember the あ part but let's include the う as well for this one. Who do you want to meet more than anyone? Think about it. Then, imagine meeting them. The first thing they do is grab your arm and pinch it. You yell out " OW !" ( あう ) and they laugh and run away.

sentences.english: to meet for the first time
I'm meeting my mother in the United States.

sentences.japanese: 兄とは大体、月に一回会います。
sentences.english: I usually meet my older brother once a month.

sentences.japanese: トーフグのコウイチに生で会ったことある？
sentences.english: Have you ever met Koichi from Tofugu in-person?

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means mix so the verb version is to mix something . It’s transitive, so you’re doing the mixing. With this word, the things you’ve mixed are still distinguishable from each other. Two types of fish in your aquarium, books of different genres on your shelf — that kind of thing.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Who always said not to mix your white and red socks in the laundry? That would be your Ma ( ま ).

sentences.english: to mix three colors of thread

sentences.japanese: カードをよく交ぜて下さい。
男の子と女の子を交ぜたクラスでした。
sentences.english: The class was a mix of boys and girls.

sentences.japanese: 日本人、フランス人、イギリス人を交ぜた女子サッカーチームに入った。
sentences.english: I joined a women's soccer team with a mix of Japanese, French, and British players.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means times . There's no good verb for the word "times" but you can probably imagine something doing something over and over and over again. What word would represent this? It would be to revolve , to go around , or to rotate . Bear in mind that this verb is intransitive, so it happens on its own. Something revolves or rotates, all by itself.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have a bag of walnuts that you're bringing to a friend's house but you trip and drop them all on the ground. You shout, " Mah Wa lnuts! ( まわ )" as they start to revolve around you on the ground. Picture your walnuts going around you, getting all dirty.

sentences.japanese: テーブルの上で、コインが回る。
sentences.english: The coin spins on the table.

sentences.japanese: スシには、「回るスシ」と「回らないスシ」二つのタイプがあります。
sentences.english: There are two types of sushi. "Sushi that goes around" and "sushi that doesn't go around".

sentences.japanese: 去年のバレンタインはクラス中を回って女子からチョコレートをもらった。
sentences.english: Last year on Valentine's day I went around the class and got chocolates from girls.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means run so now you know the verb version of that is to run .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: You have to remember the はし portion. Think of yourself running. It's nice. As you run, though, you notice the ground changing into something weird and mushy. Everything is turning into hash ( はし ) browns. You start to get sucked in, and soon you can't run anymore. Smell the hash browns and taste them too. What a terrible run this was.

sentences.japanese: マラソンコースを走る
ガードレールの上を走る
町の北を走るバスがあります。
sentences.english: There is a bus that runs north of town.

sentences.japanese: 毎日走って会社に行く人生はもうイヤなんです。
sentences.english: I can't take a life of having to run to the office every day anymore.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means say , so the verb version of that is to say .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: To remember the reading い we use the word "eagle." You're trying to say something, but every time you try to say anything an ea gle ( い ) swoops down and pecks at your face then flies away. Just imagine yourself saying tiny bits of words, then an eagle crashing down on your face. Then, you wait in silence. Nothing happens. You try to say something again, and the eagle swoops down on you again.

sentences.japanese: スタッフは「ありがとうございました」と、言う。
もう少しゆっくり言って下さい。
sentences.english: Please say it a little slower.

sentences.japanese: 今日はちゃんと先生に「おはようございます」言った？
sentences.english: Did you tell your teacher "Good morning" today?

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "stand" and this means to stand something up . It also can mean to make something , both in a physical sense, like making a sound, and a mental sense, like making a plan. Don't confuse this with 立つ . 立てる means that you're standing something up. As in, "I stood up the action figure" or "I will erect the flag." You're doing the action to something else.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned the kun'yomi reading for this kanji with 立つ , so you should be good to go!

sentences.english: to set something up a little

sentences.japanese: スケジュールを立てる

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means stop , so the verb 止まる means to stop . But this is the intransitive version, so it doesn't take a direct object. A train stops, or you stop at a red light. See? No direct object. You can remember this because you often have to stop when you see a 丸 ( まる ), a.k.a. a circle. Think about it — red lights, the cancel symbol, and no trespassing signs are all 丸 . Even stop signs are… sort of 丸 ?
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading when you learned the 止める , so you should be able to read it already!

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 出る means "to exit," and this is the transitive version of that. In other words, you're doing the action of causing something else to exit, so this word means to take out . When you take something out, you're making it exit where it previously was, right? 出す is a super versatile word that can also mean to turn in (an assignment, for example), to put out something (like the garbage or recycling), or to let out something (a sigh, a sound, or even a bodily fluid). It can also be a casual term for paying for something, since you're taking out your cash and handing it over.
readingMnemonic: The だ reading is the part you want to remember here, so here's a mnemonic to help you out: Your favorite thing to take out is your da d's ( だ ) credit card. You take it out whenever it's time for a shopping spree — which is all the time, basically. Your dad's okay with this, although you sometimes cause him to let out a wail when he sees his monthly statement. Thanks, Daddy — love you!

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means think , so the verb version is to think about or to consider . Note that this isn't the "to think" that is like "I think that he is a power ranger." No, this is more like the actual thinking action. That's why this word is "to think about" or "to consider" rather than plain old "to think" which is 思う .

meaningMnemonic: This word means to understand , which might surprise you if you remember that the kanji 分 means part . Think of it this way: to understand something you have to break it down into its parts to see how it works. Watch out, though, because whereas in English you understand something, in Japanese the thing you understand is the grammatical subject (it's doing the action). So, a more literal meaning for this is to be understandable . In other words, there's no object, and 分かる is intransitive, meaning it happens on its own. The かる ending is a hint, because verbs with かる as okurigana (kana added to the kanji) are usually intransitive.
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Whenever you try to understand something, you just start screaming " WAAAAAAAAAHHHH " ( わ ). It helps you focus and concentrate on what you’re trying to understand, to the dismay of everyone around you. WAAAAAAAAAHHHH.

readingMnemonic: The reading is also an exception. It can be いき , but instead we're focusing on the ゆき reading. meaningMnemonic: The 々 character just repeats the kanji before it. In other words: color , color ! But think figuratively, here — something with lots of different colors like this could also be described as various , which is exactly what this word means. 色々 used to mean a variety of colors, but over time evolved into a more general word for a diverse variety of something. You'll often see it as an adjective, like 色々な人 (various people), but it also pops up when talking about mixed experiences or actions, as in 色々あったね (a lot happened) or 色々考えた (I thought about it in all kinds of ways). Kind of appropriate how this word has various uses, eh?
